I'm tallying the areas of these four pieces (4, 5, 7, 5) totaling 21 squares, then checking which piece to remove so the remainder forms a clean rectangle — testing removing the 4-piece leaves 17 (prime, won't work), so I'm now trying removing the 1-piece to see if the remaining 16 squares tile a 4x4 rectangle.

Removing the 7-piece leaves 14 squares, which I test against a 2x7 or 7x2 rectangle, but the shapes' heights don't fit cleanly, so that fails. Then I try removing the 5-piece: fitting the 7-piece into a 4x4 grid, then placing the 1-piece and 4-piece into the remaining cells — and it works out perfectly, confirming removing the 5-piece is the answer.

content.text:
I need to design inputs where exactly one removal works, so I'm testing a setup with two 2x2 squares plus an odd L-tromino piece — removing the L leaves two squares that tile a 2x4 rectangle, but removing a square leaves 7 cells which is prime and fails.

Now I'm trying a second design: three 1x3 bars plus an odd S-tetromino intended to tile a 3x3 region. Removing the S leaves exactly 9 cells forming the 3x3 as needed, but I'm checking whether removing a bar instead (leaving two bars plus the S, 10 cells) could tile a 2x5 or 5x2 rectangle by testing various shifted placements of the S shape — and after working through the cases, none of them let the bars fill the remaining space, confirming this construction also has a unique valid removal.

I'm now considering a third design using domino pairs, testing whether three horizontal dominoes could tile a 2x3 block (they can't, since a leftover vertical pair remains), then trying four dominoes tiling a 2x4 block instead, which works cleanly, so I'll build a third demo around that structure plus an odd piece.

For that demo, I'm choosing two 1x4 bars in different colors that together fill a 2x4 grid, and pairing them with a plus-shaped pentomino as the odd piece that would overflow a too-small grid, confirming the sizing works out correctly. I also want to make sure the output grids vary in size across the demos.
